sources.citation: Lynch, John, Malcolm Ross & Terry Crowley. 2002. The Oceanic Languages. Richmond: Curzon. Sect. 5.2 'Utupua and Vanikoro'; family tree; Tryon's Buma (Vanikoro) sketch.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on Tanimbili: the name occurs once, in the Utupua-Vanikoro family tree; Utupua is discussed only for subgrouping. The only Temotu sketch is Buma (Vanikoro), whose penultimate-stress statement is for a different island and subgroup, not applicable.

sources.citation: Tryon, Darrell T. & B. D. Hackman. 1983. Solomon Islands Languages: An Internal Classification (Pacific Linguistics C-72). Canberra: ANU. Tanimbili = wordlist no. 101 (Utupua), 50 speakers; name index (Tanabile, Tanambile, Tanebile, Gnisunggu); Utupua/Vanikoro reflex tables.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Silent. Tanimbili appears in the census, name index, POC reflex tables (e.g. *niuR > Tanimbili nonio) and 300-item wordlist rows without stress marks; 'penultimate' does not occur; the only 'stress' tokens are 'It is stressed however' (rhetorical) and footnotes 'in unstressed position' on vowel reflexes of other languages.

sources.citation: Ray, Sidney H. 1926. A Comparative Study of the Melanesian Island Languages. Cambridge: CUP. 'Grammar of the Utupua Language', pp. 461-469 (= Asumboa [aua], from a MS by Rev. B. Teilo).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: open copy online; also held in print at Harvard (Widener Library (offsite storage), call number 2234.7.25)
sources.note: Describes Asumboa, not Tanimbili; its 'Alphabet' and 'Sounds' sections carry no accent or stress statement.

sources.note: The only modern first-hand treatment of the three Utupua languages (Nembao, Asumboa, Tanimbili) by the only linguist who collected Tanimbili data; contains sound-correspondence tables (Google Books index) and may include phonological notes on stress. Google's index shows 'Tanimbili' and 'penultimate' both occur in the volume, unverified whether in the same passage.
